## Overview:
The PR replaces one `db.users.find(id)` query per input ID with a deduplicated bulk `findMany` query. It then indexes results by ID and reconstructs the original input order, including duplicates and `null` for missing users.

High-level risks for specialist review include ORM behavior for empty `in` lists, large ID batches, and whether bulk-query consistency or missing-record semantics exactly match the prior per-ID behavior. No clear direct-diff P3/nit candidates are visible.

## Strengths:
- Reduces database round trips by batching lookups.
- Deduplicates IDs before querying.
- Preserves input ordering and duplicate entries.
- Explicitly handles missing rows with `null`.

resolvedReview.overview:
This PR rewrites `loadUsers` in `src/users.ts` from one `db.users.find(id)` query per input ID (`Promise.all` over N queries) to a single batched `db.users.findMany({ where: { id: { in: uniqueIds } } })` call. IDs are deduplicated through a `Set` before querying, results are indexed into a `Map` keyed by `row.id`, and the original input order — including duplicate entries — is reconstructed with `?? null` substituting for missing users.

The change is a genuine performance improvement (N round trips → 1) and the core mapping logic is correct for the common cases. However, the PR body claims "preserving existing contracts," and the review surfaced a few real behavioral deltas: empty input now hits the database, the caller's array is re-read after the await, and unbounded `IN`-list size introduces a new failure mode at scale. None are blocking; all are cheap to fix.

findings.title: [P2] Short-circuit empty ID lists before querying
findings.body: With `ids = []`, the old `Promise.all([].map(...))` resolved to `[]` without touching `db`. The new code always calls `findMany({ where: { id: { in: [] } } })`, which both issues a pointless query and adds a new DB-failure surface for empty input — and some adapters reject empty `IN` lists outright. Flagged independently by four review lanes. Add an early `return []` (or confirm the adapter short-circuits empty lists).

findings.title: [P2] Snapshot `ids` before awaiting `findMany`
findings.body: The old `ids.map(...)` ran synchronously before any await, freezing the ID list at call time. Line 25 now re-reads the caller-owned mutable array *after* the `findMany` await. If the caller mutates `ids` while the query is in flight (adds, removes, reorders), the returned array no longer matches what was queried — e.g., an added ID silently becomes `null`. Snapshot the array at function entry (`const idsSnapshot = [...ids]`) and map over the snapshot.

findings.title: [P2] Chunk the `IN` lookup below the backend parameter limit
findings.body: The single generated statement binds every unique ID, so inputs exceeding the backend's limit (e.g., ~999 on older SQLite, 2100 on SQL Server, 65535 on Postgres) now fail the entire call, where the previous per-ID queries hit no single-statement limit. Downgraded from P1 by the orchestrator because the threshold is backend- and workload-dependent with no in-repo evidence of such call volumes. Consider batching `uniqueIds` into bounded chunks while preserving the order-reconstruction logic.

findings.title: [P3] Confirm the missing-user sentinel change
findings.body: The old code returned whatever `db.users.find(id)` resolved to for a missing ID; the new `byId.get(id) ?? null` normalizes that to `null`. `db` is an ambient global with no in-repo definition, so this cannot be proven a contract change — but if `find` resolved `undefined`, strict-equality/serialization consumers now observe `null`. Worth confirming intended given the PR's "preserving existing contracts" claim.

findings.title: [P3] Add regression coverage for the batched mapping
findings.body: The new semantics have several edge cases — order preservation, duplicate-ID reconstruction, missing-user substitution, and the empty-input path — and the repository has no tests verifying any of them. A regression in the mapping logic would go undetected.

findings.title: [nit] Build the Map without the intermediate tuple array
findings.body: `rows.map(row => [row.id, row])` allocates an O(rows) intermediate array plus one two-element tuple per row before `Map` construction. A plain `for` loop populating the map directly avoids the peak allocations — purely optional, the current form is idiomatic.

# PR Review

**Verdict:** approve

## Overview

This PR rewrites `loadUsers` in `src/users.ts` from one `db.users.find(id)` query per input ID (`Promise.all` over N queries) to a single batched `db.users.findMany({ where: { id: { in: uniqueIds } } })` call. IDs are deduplicated through a `Set` before querying, results are indexed into a `Map` keyed by `row.id`, and the original input order — including duplicate entries — is reconstructed with `?? null` substituting for missing users.

The change is a genuine performance improvement (N round trips → 1) and the core mapping logic is correct for the common cases. However, the PR body claims "preserving existing contracts," and the review surfaced a few real behavioral deltas: empty input now hits the database, the caller's array is re-read after the await, and unbounded `IN`-list size introduces a new failure mode at scale. None are blocking; all are cheap to fix.

## Verification

Verification was **disabled**: no user-level `verificationBaselines` are configured (`pr_review_verify` list returned none), so no baseline executed against head `a749b53374fadd0c5381b6ebbb7e81ca725912ff`. Disclosure: verification executes PR code unsandboxed (no filesystem/network containment; supervision covers only the original POSIX process group); an external sandbox/container wrapper is recommended for untrusted PRs if enabled later.

## Findings

### [P2] Short-circuit empty ID lists before querying
**Severity:** P2
**Rationale:** With `ids = []`, the old `Promise.all([].map(...))` resolved to `[]` without touching `db`. The new code always calls `findMany({ where: { id: { in: [] } } })`, which both issues a pointless query and adds a new DB-failure surface for empty input — and some adapters reject empty `IN` lists outright. Flagged independently by four review lanes. Add an early `return []` (or confirm the adapter short-circuits empty lists).
**Location:** `src/users.ts:23 RIGHT`

### [P2] Snapshot `ids` before awaiting `findMany`
**Severity:** P2
**Rationale:** The old `ids.map(...)` ran synchronously before any await, freezing the ID list at call time. Line 25 now re-reads the caller-owned mutable array *after* the `findMany` await. If the caller mutates `ids` while the query is in flight (adds, removes, reorders), the returned array no longer matches what was queried — e.g., an added ID silently becomes `null`. Snapshot the array at function entry (`const idsSnapshot = [...ids]`) and map over the snapshot.
**Location:** `src/users.ts:25 RIGHT`

### [P2] Chunk the `IN` lookup below the backend parameter limit
**Severity:** P2
**Rationale:** The single generated statement binds every unique ID, so inputs exceeding the backend's limit (e.g., ~999 on older SQLite, 2100 on SQL Server, 65535 on Postgres) now fail the entire call, where the previous per-ID queries hit no single-statement limit. Downgraded from P1 by the orchestrator because the threshold is backend- and workload-dependent with no in-repo evidence of such call volumes. Consider batching `uniqueIds` into bounded chunks while preserving the order-reconstruction logic.
**Location:** `src/users.ts:23 RIGHT`

### [P3] Confirm the missing-user sentinel change
**Severity:** P3
**Rationale:** The old code returned whatever `db.users.find(id)` resolved to for a missing ID; the new `byId.get(id) ?? null` normalizes that to `null`. `db` is an ambient global with no in-repo definition, so this cannot be proven a contract change — but if `find` resolved `undefined`, strict-equality/serialization consumers now observe `null`. Worth confirming intended given the PR's "preserving existing contracts" claim.
**Location:** `src/users.ts:25 RIGHT`

### [P3] Add regression coverage for the batched mapping
**Severity:** P3
**Rationale:** The new semantics have several edge cases — order preservation, duplicate-ID reconstruction, missing-user substitution, and the empty-input path — and the repository has no tests verifying any of them. A regression in the mapping logic would go undetected.
**Location:** `src/users.ts:22-25 RIGHT`

### [nit] Build the Map without the intermediate tuple array
**Severity:** nit
**Rationale:** `rows.map(row => [row.id, row])` allocates an O(rows) intermediate array plus one two-element tuple per row before `Map` construction. A plain `for` loop populating the map directly avoids the peak allocations — purely optional, the current form is idiomatic.
**Location:** `src/users.ts:24 RIGHT`

## Lane completeness

All requested lanes completed. The `security-performance` lane's first dispatch returned `partial` (raw evidence: no findings); it was rerun to completion with the same tool policy and confirmed **NO FINDINGS** — no injection, query-construction, or data-exposure regressions were substantiated in the changed code. All other five lanes (`overview`, `conventions-maintainability`, `correctness`, `correctness-contracts`, `performance-resources`) completed on first dispatch.

## Strengths and notes

- **Correctness:** The core batched-lookup logic is sound for the common case — dedupe, Map indexing, and order/duplicate reconstruction are all implemented correctly; the flagged deltas are edge conditions (empty input, concurrent mutation of the input array, oversized lists), not core-logic errors.
- **Security:** No security regressions found; IDs flow into a structured `where` clause, not raw query construction.
- **Performance:** Clear win — N queries collapsed to 1 with deduplication reducing list size further; the `IN`-limit and empty-input notes above are the only scalability caveats.
- **Notes:** All findings are non-blocking; the empty-input early return and the `ids` snapshot are both one-line fixes that would fully align the implementation with the PR's stated "preserving existing contracts" intent.
